Documentary · Personal Narrative

The Camera Forever
Changed My Life

A journey shaped by creativity, uncertainty, and the search for something real

01 — The story

Karsten was just a kid with a camera trying to understand what was going on before the film projects, the all-night editing sessions, and before anyone started referring to him as a filmmaker. Karsten didn't know where he was heading. All he knew was that he wanted to capture something that seemed valuable, although he couldn't quite figure out the reason why.

Spencer (Karsten's best friend) remembers when Karsten never even referred to himself as a filmmaker. When "everyone else was shooting on iPods," Spencer saw that Karsten had this camera that could blur the background and pull the world into focus. Spencer saw the lens moving in and out and knew this kid knows what he's doing. It wasn't a plan. It wasn't a resume. It was a spark.

"This kid knows what he's doing."

Karsten can look back to his middle school days, to nights spent watching Casey Neistat's vlogs with a dream of a life in front of the camera. While his curiosity was the spark, his interest became an obsession. He was filming all the time, editing for hours on end, and pursuing a feeling he couldn't put his finger on.

Karsten's studio — the instruments that bridge film and sound

When Karsten got to college, his curiosity had developed into a discipline. He worked through his projects, filming all the sports at the University of Kentucky, building a life that resembled a career. The camera was no longer just a tool. It was a way to understand his world.

This perspective was influenced as much by challenge as by opportunity. As challenges in his life arose, the work became more than just an ambition. It became a way of making sense of the world that didn't always come with explanations for the moments as they unfolded.

A hobby turned professional when he started filming at the University of Kentucky. It was during his time filming for Kentucky Sports Video that Karsten realized his love of the camera had transformed into something much more. "They liked everything I was doing," he said. "I guess they believed in me more than I believed in myself."

"I guess they believed in me more than I believed in myself."

By the time of his graduation, Karsten was more than a person skilled at making videos; he had become a cinematographer with his own distinct vision. The long hours, frequent changes in scenery, and the need to document important events made him mature. His initial struggle to find his footing in an uncertain world had eventually developed into a career and an everyday means of living.

Post-graduation saw the end of that structure and presented him with a whole new set of challenges. As a freelance videographer, Karsten needed to rely on himself for everything. There was no safety net to cushion him from any falls. However, it gave him one thing he had not had before — the freedom to do whatever he wanted creatively.

Music isn't an art form distinct from filmmaking, according to Karsten. It has become an extension of the same instinct. The goal remains the same: "How am I going to make someone feel something?" However, the response isn't coming in the form of imagery alone anymore; it's being found in sound. It's a trial-and-error approach that allows him to play around without overthinking and chase the sounds that he wants.

It's the same concept that producer Rick Rubin always emphasizes when speaking about creativity — that notion of creating the way a child does, free from all doubts and complications, is exactly what Karsten is starting to embrace. Sometimes things don't need to be perfect. They don't even have to be understandable at first. They just have to be authentic.

"I'm going to keep doing my silly little videos and my silly little songs, and I hope it gets me where I want to go."

There is no end in sight, which is the whole idea.
